questions.prompt: An npn has \(I_S = 5\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{A}\). What is \(I_C\) (in µA) at \(V_{BE} = 0.65\ \mathrm{V}\), with \(V_{th} = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\)?
questions.figure_alt: Collector current versus base-emitter voltage: an exponential that is negligible below about 0.6 V and then rises steeply.

questions.prompt: On the \(I_C\)-\(V_{CE}\) family of curves (one curve per base current), what does the flat part of each curve show?
options: The forward-active region, where \(I_C\) is set by \(I_B\) (or \(V_{BE}\)) and nearly independent of \(V_{CE}\)
Saturation, where the transistor acts as a closed switch
questions.explanation: Above a few tenths of a volt, the collector collects whatever the emitter injects: \(I_C = \beta_FI_B\), almost independent of \(V_{CE}\) (reader Sec. 11.3.2).
questions.figure_alt: Family of BJT collector curves: for each fixed base current, I_C rises quickly near V_CE = 0 and then stays nearly flat; equal steps in I_B give equal steps in I_C.

questions.prompt: A BJT has \(\beta_F = 150\). What base current (in µA) gives \(I_C = 1.2\ \mathrm{mA}\)?
questions.figure_alt: Family of BJT collector curves: for each fixed base current, I_C rises quickly near V_CE = 0 and then stays nearly flat; equal steps in I_B give equal steps in I_C.

questions.prompt: By how many mV must \(V_{BE}\) increase to raise \(I_C\) by a factor of 10 (\(V_{th} = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\))?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta V_{BE} = V_{th}\ln10 \approx 59.9\ \mathrm{mV}\): the familiar 60 mV per decade.
questions.figure_alt: Collector current versus base-emitter voltage: an exponential that is negligible below about 0.6 V and then rises steeply.

questions.prompt: A transistor carries \(I_C = 0.4\ \mathrm{mA}\) at \(V_{BE} = 0.68\ \mathrm{V}\). What \(V_{BE}\) (in V) gives \(I_C = 2\ \mathrm{mA}\)?
questions.figure_alt: Collector current versus base-emitter voltage: an exponential that is negligible below about 0.6 V and then rises steeply.

questions.prompt: When \(V_{CE}\) drops very low (say 0.1 V) with \(V_{BE} = 0.7\ \mathrm{V}\), the collector curve falls steeply. Why?
options: The base-collector junction becomes forward biased (saturation), so the collector starts injecting back
questions.explanation: \(V_{BC} = V_{BE} - V_{CE} = 0.6\ \mathrm{V}\): the collector diode turns on and opposes the forward current. That steep region is saturation.
questions.figure_alt: Family of BJT collector curves: for each fixed base current, I_C rises quickly near V_CE = 0 and then stays nearly flat; equal steps in I_B give equal steps in I_C.

questions.prompt: Equal steps in base current produce what on the \(I_C\)-\(V_{CE}\) family?
options: Curves that bunch together at high current
Equally spaced curves, since \(I_C = \beta_FI_B\) is linear
questions.explanation: \(I_C\) is linear in \(I_B\) but exponential in \(V_{BE}\). Equal \(V_{BE}\) steps give exponentially spaced curves instead.
questions.figure_alt: Family of BJT collector curves: for each fixed base current, I_C rises quickly near V_CE = 0 and then stays nearly flat; equal steps in I_B give equal steps in I_C.

questions.prompt: In the flat region, one curve rises from \(1.00\ \mathrm{mA}\) at \(V_{CE} = 2\ \mathrm{V}\) to \(1.05\ \mathrm{mA}\) at \(V_{CE} = 7\ \mathrm{V}\). Extrapolating the line back to \(I_C = 0\), at what negative \(V_{CE}\) does it hit the axis (give the magnitude, in V)?
questions.explanation: Slope \(= 0.05/5 = 0.01\ \mathrm{mA/V}\). The line reaches zero \(1.00/0.01 = 100\ \mathrm{V}\) to the left of 2 V, at \(-98\ \mathrm{V}\). That intercept magnitude is the Early voltage \(V_A\).
questions.figure_alt: Family of BJT collector curves: for each fixed base current, I_C rises quickly near V_CE = 0 and then stays nearly flat; equal steps in I_B give equal steps in I_C.

questions.prompt: Preview of transistor action: why is \(I_C\) exponential in \(V_{BE}\)?
options: \(V_{BE}\) sets the injected minority-electron density at the base edge through the law of the junction, and \(I_C\) is the diffusion current that density drives
questions.explanation: Just like a diode: \(n_p(0) = n_{p0}e^{V_{BE}/V_{th}}\), and the collector current is \(qD_n\) times the gradient across the base.
questions.figure_alt: Collector current versus base-emitter voltage: an exponential that is negligible below about 0.6 V and then rises steeply.

questions.prompt: Preview of the BJT small-signal model: at \(I_C = 0.52\ \mathrm{mA}\), what is the transconductance \(g_m = I_C/V_{th}\) in mS?
questions.explanation: \(g_m = 0.52\ \mathrm{mA}/26\ \mathrm{mV} = 20\ \mathrm{mS}\), the slope of the exponential \(I_C\)-\(V_{BE}\) curve.

questions.prompt: Preview of the Early effect: why do the 'flat' collector curves actually slope upward slightly?
options: Higher \(V_{CE}\) widens the collector depletion region, narrowing the effective base and steepening the electron gradient
questions.explanation: Base-width modulation, the BJT version of channel-length modulation.
questions.figure_alt: Family of BJT collector curves: for each fixed base current, I_C rises quickly near V_CE = 0 and then stays nearly flat; equal steps in I_B give equal steps in I_C.
